answer:
1000 SCFM of natural gas is about 1607 Nm³/h, or roughly 1610 Nm³/h.

I'm assuming the usual US gas-industry standard conditions for SCFM (60 °F and 14.696 psia) and 0 °C and 1.01325 bar for Nm³. The figures were computed, not looked up:

- 1000 ft³/min × 60 = 60,000 ft³/h, and × 0.0283168 m³/ft³ = 1699.0 m³/h at standard conditions.
- Correcting the temperature from 60 °F to 0 °C (273.15 / 288.706 = 0.94612) gives **1607.5 Nm³/h**. The pressure is the same on both sides, so it needs no correction.

The answer depends on which "standard" the SCFM figure uses:

| SCFM basis | Nm³/h |
|---|---|
| 60 °F, 14.696 psia (most common) | 1607.5 |
| 60 °F, 14.73 psia (AGA / US gas billing) | 1611.2 |
| 68 °F, 14.696 psia | 1583.1 |

This treats natural gas as an ideal gas. Its compressibility factor is about 0.998 at both reference states, so the ratio between them changes by much less than 0.1% (I did not calculate this). The conversion factor is about 1.607 Nm³/h per SCFM. No files were created.
